#4260. Deadlock Bot Farms Begin to Plague Ranked

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

All multiplayer games want to maximize their player count, and most focus on splitting the hypercompetitive and the casual away from each other in unique modes. Over the years, titles have had to find unique ways to keep competitive modes accessible without letting in any ne'er-do-wells, with varying success.

Sony is keeping its exclusives at home for the foreseeable future, denying PC ports for new and upcoming PlayStation titles.

Deadlock’s second season of ranked play just opened, and with it a rework to the way players unlock characters. Now, players don’t need to win matches, just complete enough on a hero to amass points for ranked selection.

With this change in place, multiple bot farms have opened up, slowly gathering points and ruining games to sell those same accounts to potential buyers once they’re ranked and ready.

Deadlock’s initial ranked system was a bit restrictive, requiring players to win a sizable 15 games on any hero they planned to play with, alongside 60 overall wins. Three separate heroes needed to surpass this 15-game milestone, making losses feel awful and progress feel slow.

On the bright side, the steep requirements made the process very difficult for any account resellers, requiring them to actually play out their games to win if they wanted accounts to flourish. With the change to a points-based system following ranked beta season 2, accounts have begun to set up dummy bots in matches, doing just enough to avoid getting AFK kicked without providing any benefit to the team.

Valve itself has dealt with this issue before, with a couple of different methods throughout its myriad titles. For Team Fortress 2, they let the game sit for a long while, suffering as bots, both subtle and egregious, dominated the game. Bots are still abundant in the class shooter, though stricter bot detection software has helped curb their numbers.

Over the years, titles have had to find unique ways to keep competitive modes accessible without letting in any ner-do-wells, with varying success.

CSGO and CSGO 2 both implemented a system incentivizing players to make a one-time purchase for “premium matchmaking”, alongside the occasional reward of a crate. Through this, actual players and those attempting to bot accounts are separated, as accounts aren't typically very expensive, and the cost of matchmaking can quickly add up for multiple profiles.

With more faces joining Deadlock all the time, ensuring access to the ranked playlist without letting in too many bots will be paramount, but I honestly think the old win system worked perfectly. It took a while to unlock heroes, but it ensured you knew how to pilot and win on your pick when you eventually made it to ranked. With this new bot epidemic surging, Valve has a short window to close the gap.

This has been a serious case of the absolute bummer cheat makers and bot runners continuing to be in online games, leaping at any chance for player convenience to spoil it for everyone else. We’ve seen this plague online games for decades, even as developers continue to find new ways to fight back.

Whether its spinbotters on Hightower or macros for hard inputs in MOBAs, the best policy seems to be making the process of getting to ranked just annoying enough to dissuade cheaters, either through small payments or sheer time. Either way, those who are really here to appreciate the game are more than willing to put in the time, as long as they feel Valve is attempting to solve the issue.

Valve is riding a massive high off of the City Never Sleeps update for Deadlock, and the only way they could realistically lose that momentum is if they fumble their answer to these bots. Making that mistake cursed TF2 for months of nigh unplayability, and if Valve aims to turn Deadlock into their next big thing, they can’t afford to fumble.

#4259. Diablo 4's long-awaited Tower and its Leaderboards enter beta today, and there's no PTR funny business this time

Diablo 4's first big moment of 2026 is nearly upon us, and it's one feature many have been looking forward to for actual years.

Diablo 4 is about to deliver on Blizzard’s years-old promise to add a challenging, leaderboard-driven experience to the action RPG. The beta for The Tower, and its associated Leaderboards are about to kick off.

As recently revealed, the new experience launches today at 11am PT, 2pm ET, 7pm GMT. This is a beta version that arrives alongside update 2.5.2.

This early launch won’t offer the full experience, and it’s mainly designed to get it into the hands of players early so that Blizzard could get as much feedback as possible and incorporate it into the final version.

The beta is available to everyone, which is a nice change from the usual rigmarole players would have to go through to get the PTR build and play on a different branch. The Tower, and Leaderboards will be available only in the Seasonal Realm, however. Indeed, the plan is to build on what’s there with each future season, so it’s best to think of it as a seasonal experience.

The Tower is about as simple of an activity as you can get in an action RPG. The goal is to climb as many floors as you can as quickly as you can, all while battling increasingly difficult mobs.

You need to reach and beat the Tower’s final boss before you can call it a run. The Leaderboard will then show your time, and let you see how well you did compared to other players.

The Tower is available to anyone who completed Rank 2 of the current Season Rank. Once done, an Obelisk will appear in Cerrigar, letting you access the challenge.

The Leaderboards themselves will operate on a two-week schedule, all of which will take place during a given season. In this case, they’re going to close the day before Season of the Divine Interversion - the game’s current season - ends.

Blizzard published an updated set of patch notes that show how much has changed since The Tower, and Leaderboards first became playable in the patch 2.5.0 PTR.

Though the two new additions have been anticipated for a while, there’s not been much exciting going on in the world of Diablo 4, apart, of course, from the surprise arrival of The Paladin class, which became available in December last year to coincide with the announcement of Lord of Hatred, the game’s next expansion.

#4256. The Sims developer vows "our values are unchanged," as it teases multiple projects from post-Saudi-owned EA

The team behind one of EA's most diverse franchises has issued a statement about its future under the soon-to-be Saudi-owned publisher.

In their (slightly belated) new years message to players, the developer of EA’s The Sims series of games has lightly addressed concerns about its future within the publisher in a wide-ranging letter to the community.

The letter also serves as something of a light plan for what players can expect soon, and in the future, alongside what the various teams are currently working on.

The developer starts off the yearly check-in with a statement that attempts to address concerns about the future of The Sims, historically one of EA’s most inclusive and culturally diverse franchises.

This, of course, comes in the wake of last year’s bombshell that EA is being taken private by a coalition led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), alongside investment firms Silver Lake Capital and Affinity Partners. The $55 billion acquisition was approved by EA’s shareholders in December, and is set to close by the end of June.

Understandably, many raised concerns about what EA’s new ownership would mean for its people, and portfolio of games. The news is concerning for The Sims in particular, a series that’s long embraced diversity and inclusivity, and has historically been popular among women, people of colour, and members of the LGBTQ+ community.

“Our Sims team's creative control, guided by our values of inclusivity, choice, creativity, community, and play, has not changed,” the post reads, though without referring to the buyout directly at any point.

“These values inspire the decisions we make each and every day as we plan for today, tomorrow, and the future.”

As for what’s to come in 2026 and beyond, it sounds like The Sims team has multiple irons in the fire. The developer is working on “a family of new Sims experiences” that will find homes on PC, console, and mobile. Crucially, the post says that not every experience will be on every platform, in order for each to focus on delivering something different and interesting.

Future releases, of course, include new The Sims 4 content that focuses on the single-player experience. The social and more multiplayer-driven experiences, however, will instead be found in Project Rene, the mobile-first life-sim currently in development. (Despite early confidence that it was a working title for The Sims 5, it's now confirmed that Project Rene won’t, in fact, be a direct successor to The Sims 4.)

Some of these projects will see more playtesting throughout 2026, so you should probably sign up for The Sims Labs if you want to hear about when/how you can get involved.

As for the next single-player Assassin’s Creed, Codename Hexe, Ubisoft says it will share the next major update on this game in 2027. First announced in 2022, Codename Hexe is set during the 17th-century reign of the Holy Roman Empire, and the era's witch hunts will play a significant role.

With the release of Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced earlier this year, Ubisoft has given fans what they'll likely see as a disappointing update on potential future remakes: “One thing we want to be transparent about today is that we currently have no other Assassin's Creed remake actively in development. Our teams are already focused on the next chapter of Assassin's Creed titles, including projects you haven't heard about yet, featuring new settings and stories.”

However, Ubisoft adds that this door isn’t closed for good. “Like many of you, we love the idea of revisiting our classic titles, and we'll keep exploring opportunities to bring older titles back,” says Ubisoft.

Ubisoft’s next update concerns the live-action Assassin's Creed series in production for Netflix. They say the show is “nearing completion” in Rome and that award-winning composer Hannah Peel (Insomnia, Rogue Agent, Game of Thrones: The Last Watch) is composing the score.

Lastly, Ubisoft teases big celebrations are planned for 2027, which marks the 20th anniversary of the Assassin's Creed franchise. It's keeping details to itself for now, but states it's "preparing a year of reveals, updates, rewards, and community moments. "

For more on Assassin's Creed, check out our review of Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced.

#4249. 10 Pokémon That Are the Biggest Red Flags

Aden Carter is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2020. He specializes in lists and guides, with a focus on RPGs, horror games, survival horror, Soulslikes, cozy/sim games, and action-adventure titles. Before joining DualShockers, Aden contributed to GameRant, XDA, Gamepur, I

There are over 1,000 Pokémon now and they span nine generations of games. Over the years, there have been many Pokémon designs, with some of them being fantastic, and others being rather… questionable.

With that being said, everyone has a favorite Pokémon, but not all of them convey a positive or welcoming message. In fact, some of them are serious red flags to have as your favorite.

These Pokémon will make others cringe for obvious reasons, and possibly even question your taste. Sometimes it is about the Pokémon’s look, other times the Pokédex is to blame, and you can even blame society for others.

Charizard has been around since the beginning of the Pokémon series, and it quickly became a Pokémon that was beloved by everyone. Many of us were around to see Ash take in Charmander, and help it grow into a fiery beast.

However, there are many who consider Charizard to be a big red flag when choosing your favorite Pokémon. The reason for this is that you are far too basic if this is your choice.

Of course, there is a lot of context behind Charizard being a red flag. After all, it is the Pokémon that has received some of the most attention, with it getting multiple forms and promotions. It’s almost like Charizard is the mascot of Pokémon with how much attention it gets.

From the Eevee evolutions to Magikarp becoming something useful, here are the Pokémon in FireRed and LeafGreen that feel different after evolving.

The original generation of Pokémon was something that blew the minds of many kids. However, the magic that once created something that everyone loved ended up creating some rather poorly designed monsters in later generations.

One Pokémon design that felt uninspired is the Trubbish line, as it is nothing more than a bag of garbage that evolves into a pile of trash. Garbodor is nothing more than a trash pile that many associate with being smelly.

The internet ruined Garbodor by turning it into a meme where if you like the Pokémon, you are considered dirty. On the other hand, many associate this Pokémon as a red flag because choosing it feels like someone is purposefully trying to go against the grain by choosing a less universally loved Pokémon.

In past years, if you’d ask someone who their favorite Pokémon is, there was a large sect of the fan base that would say Typhlosion. He used to be cool, but everything changed when content was leaked that involved this once-innocent Pokémon.

As part of the leak in 2024, Typhlosion - specifically the Hisuian form - received some unsettling lore that involved folklore of it shapeshifting into a human and kidnapping a young girl. There’s more to it, but I don’t want to dive that deep.

Despite the leak never containing any canon information that made it into the games, and there being mistranslations, and other issues with it, Typhlosion has never really been able to escape the allegations, and so therefore, is still considered a red flag to many in the fan base.

When you bring together many people and give them the capability of being anonymous, as they can be on the internet, they have a habit of ruining everything you once loved. While there are multiple on this list, Lopunny is the first up.

Lopunny started off as Buneary - a rather adorable rabbit Pokémon - that gets an… interesting physique when it evolves into its final stage. Many saw this transformation, went online, and then proceeded to turn the Pokémon into a symbol for provocation.

Since then, it has been frowned upon whenever someone mentions that their favorite Pokémon is Lopunny, and the addition of Mega Lopunny did not help. Instead, it made things a bit worse.

Mr. Mime was an unsettling Pokémon when kids were introduced to it in the anime. Its human-like appearance mixed with a mime is something that is uncanny. However, it has only gotten worse over the years.

Digging through its Pokédex entries, you learn that it is capable of creating physical objects that are invisible. Along with that, if you interrupt its performance, it feels the need to slap you with its big flat hands.

This alone is weird, but you can add on the allegations that Mr. Mime is Ash’s stepfather in the anime. To cap it off, Mr. Mime got even more strange with the Detective Pikachu movie, further enhancing its uncanny and unsettling nature.

Did you choose Garchomp because you like the Pokémon, or did you choose it because it is a powerhouse and you are someone who gets overly competitive and sweaty during competition? Maybe it’s because you still have PTSD from Cynthia destroying you in Diamond and Pearl?

This is often what is associated with the love of Garchomp. There is no denying that Garchomp is an absolute beast of a Pokémon that can destroy others in competition, but that also makes many believe that those who like Garchomp have a far too competitive and aggressive mindset.

The other mindset people have is that Garchomp is associated with Cynthia from Diamond and Pearl. She dominated players in that era, and the idea is that those who like Garchomp haven’t gotten over that and want to inflict the same trauma on others.

There are Pokémon who have off Pokédex entries, with some of them being focused on some sort of trauma or horror story. Drifloon is one such Pokémon, with it being a ghost Pokémon who is known for kidnapping children.

The original Pokédex entries don’t make Drifloon out to be so bad, as the Dex says that it pulls on children to steal them away, but it ends up getting yanked around instead. However, this has gotten worse with time.

More recent entries specifically state that this Pokémon kidnaps children and whisks them off to the afterlife. Other entries talk about how it is specifically filled with souls and grows larger each time it steals one away. Let’s just leave this Pokémon out of our favorites list.

Pokemon Red/Blue's Lavender Town remains one of the eeriest creations in video gaming.

The internet has a way of taking any Pokémon that has slightly humanoid features and turning them into your worst nightmare. Similar to Lopunny before it, Gothitelle fell victim to those who seek to ruin things for other people.

Again, this is another Pokémon evolution line that starts off very innocent, with Gothita being a rather cute Pokémon that is very innocent in appearance. Unfortunately, that changes when it reaches its final evolution.

There is nothing innately wrong about liking this evolution line, but it definitely calls your taste into question, and many will immediately see the red flag fly, and it is completely understandable.

I am not sure that this even needs to be said because, of all the Pokémon with a humanoid appearance, Gardevoir has been treated the worst. Originally introduced in generation 3, the entire Raltz evolution line was loved, but then things went south very quickly.

Gardevoir is a Pokémon that resembles a woman in a flowing dress. Its body consists of said dress, which is more or less a flowing gown, and it has a hairstyle that appears to be done for a pageant or evening event.

However, this is enough to get the internet riled up, and Gardevoir was the first of the Pokémon of this style to be twisted by those who just seek to ruin things for other people. Now, this Pokémon is considered one of the biggest red flags of the franchise.

Eevee was, and still is, one of the most popular Pokémon there is, with many finding the little fox-like creature to be adorable. When it was introduced, it was beloved, and so were its original three evolutions; Flareon, Jolteon, and Vaporeon.

Unfortunately for Vaporeon, it became the fascination of one of the most perverse corners of the Pokémon fan base. So much so that it was treated far worse than Lopunny, Gothitelle, and Gardivoire combined.

The information about this Pokémon soon became a meme that spread like wildfire, leading to many victims being caught in the smoke. Now, many are ashamed to even talk about Vaporeon in a positive light, as it looks bad. What was once one of the most famous Pokémon of a generation has now become the biggest red flag in the fandom.

While most pokemon are friendly and nice, some are much more mischievous and ready to cause harm. Here are Pokemon ready to rob you in broad daylight

#4246. Sir Patrick Stewart, Star Trek, X-Men, And Myriad Video Games Actor, Passes Away

According to a report from The Hollywood Reporter, actor Sir Patrick Stewart has passed away at the age of 86. Stewart spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, shared that he died after “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia.”

Stewart was best known for his roles as Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation (and its various spinoffs) and Charles Xavier in the X-Men films, but he did plenty of video game performing, too. Stewart played Emperor Uriel Septim VII in The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion, one of the first characters you meet in the game, and Zobek in Castlevania: Lords of Shadow. He also played Jean-Luc Picard in about 10 different Star Trek games and Charles Xavier in five different X-Men games.

Stewart will always be a crucial voice and face in the legacy of sci-fi entertainment. Jean-Luc Picard will undoubtedly be an enduring and important character in the Star Trek franchise, and that's thanks to Stewart's portrayal of the starship captain. His portrayal of Charles Xavier also helped to legitimize the comic book movie, and he will appear again as the character in this year's upcoming Avengers: Doomsday.

Our thoughts are with his friends and family, and the millions of fans (of which I include myself) who are mourning his loss. Let's all drink some Earl Grey tea in his honor today.

#4245. After 15 years, The Sims' best spin-off finally gets its due follow-up in The Sims 4: Royalty & Legacy

The Sims Medieval had a short but powerful run back in 2011, and now many of its best features are finally coming to the main franchise.

The Sims 4 developers recently promised an exciting year for the game, and the franchise as a whole, and we just got an early look at one of those first events. After some light teasing, the developer unveiled Royalty & Legacy, the game’s next expansion.

Royalty & Legacy’s first trailer debuted on Thursday, revealing a February 12 release date, and showing off the expansion for the first time.

There’s a lot going on in Royalty & Legacy, which is priced $40. For one, it introduces a new world, Ondarion, which is going to be the setting for your kingdom, as you join a race for the throne. The expansion introduces Dynasty and Nobility - two new systems you can use to create your own world of royal shenanigans.

Ondarion is made up of three neighborhoods (regions). Each region has a unique theme and culture, and they’re each ruled by a Dynasty. Dambele is a place that prioritises art and community. Verdemar is a chaotic world of outlaws and nobles. Finally, Bellacorde is an extravagant region known for opulence and romance.

Speaking of building places, Royalty & Legacy also adds a new Lot type, The Backroom Lot. It serves two functions that change with the time of day. For instance, it can be a library or gym in the morning, and shift into a night club at night. Dambele has its own library-turned-rave, for instance.

At the heart of Ondarion are all the possible fantasy lives and stories you can live. The Sims calls them Powershifts, and they include some well-known Arthurian fantasies and other, more silly ones.

Swordsmanship is the new 10-level skill arriving with the expansion, which further plays into those fantasies by letting your Sims duel. There are even Swordsmanship Tournaments you can watch take place across every neighborhood in Ondarion.

Then there are Secret Passageways, which let you speed up moving across the new regions. They essentially let your Sims teleport between designated passageways, either on their own lots, or other lots in the world. Some of these are hidden for you to find, while others you can create.

In terms of new careers, there’s the Noble Career, where your Sim can rise through several Noble Rankings by doing basically what nobles had to do in the middle ages to earn favour.

The aforementioned Dynasty System is how you can join any of Ondarion’s existing families, or start your own. You actually have a lot of say in what goes on, including the usual business of appointing heirs.

Of course, no royal roleplay would be complete without scandals, which is where the Scandals System comes in. Through it, you can create stories to discredit others, or even topple an entire dynasty.

In November, you may recall The Sims 4 introducing new free items inspired by West African culture. In creating that content, EA worked with a group of Simmers who have direct ties to West African countries.

The group’s guidance was once again utilised to build the Dambele neighborhood in this expansion, and some of the lots around the world of Ondarion were even created by members of the group.

While you wait for Royalty & Legacy to actually arrive, there’s more in The Sims 4 you can jump in right now. The game recently kicked off a collaboration with fashion brand Coach that brought several free items to Create a Sim, and Build Buy. That arrived alongside a free update, which already makes for a busy start of the year for The Sims 4.

#4243. Death Stranding Isolations Animated Series Gets New Teaser Trailer

A new teaser trailer for Death Stranding Isolations, an upcoming animated series coming exclusively to Disney+ and Hulu next year, premiered during Kojima Productions’ 10th Anniversary Exhibition Beyond the Strand. The series was first announced last year.

Death Stranding Isolations tells an original story in the Death Stranding universe set immediately after the events of the first game. Isolations is created by Japanese animation studio E&H Production (Ninja Kamui, Bullet/Bullet, Magic Knight Rayerath) and directed by Takayuki Sano.  Death Stranding creator Hideo Kojima serves as executive producer.

Today’s teaser video provides the following story synopsis:

The Death Stranding—a catastrophic series of explosions caused when the dead crept into our world and collided with the living.

In the wake of this cataclysm, many were forced to live in absolute isolation—among them, a young girl. Although this lonely existence was forced upon her, she soon grows to prefer solitude, eschewing all opportunities for real human connection and allowing herself to be strung along by fate.

In Death Stranding, legendary game creator Hideo Kojima brought you a haunting vision of a shattered world. Now, that world expands into new frontiers with a brand-new animation series.

Under the guidance of director Takayuki Sano, world-class hand-drawn animations have been brought to life by renowned studio “E&H production” (NINJA KAMUI, BULLET/BULLET, the Magic Knight Rayearth television series).

The story is set in North America immediately after Sam—the protagonist of the game—reconnects the continent by means of the Chiral Network. However, as America is reborn from the ashes, the renewed connections that bind it together bring about new and unforeseen consequences.

In this tumultuous new landscape, there are some who walk a different path to the one chosen by Sam and his Bridges comrades: a wise old man who connects people through a method that defies all reckoning; a female soldier ensnared in a cycle of war and destruction; a boy who seethes with rage at the absurdity of his life...and of course, the girl who chose to sever all ties with the outside world...Fate has other plans for her, however, and chance encounters see her launched headfirst into a world she does not recognize.

Death Stranding Isolations is coming to Disney+ and Hulu in 2027. It’s one of the three planned big-screen adaptations of the series. An animated movie called Death Stranding: Mosquito (working title) is also in the works alongside a live-action Death Stranding film by A24.

#4242. Fortnite Officially Reveals Pirate Shop Access Drop Rates

Last week, Fortnite built itself a digital ark to weather the upcoming GTA 6 storm, introducing a new mechanic that has seen millions of players flock back to the game in the hopes of winning big: the Pirate Shop.

Pirate Shop tokens are scattered across each game, and when found, they allow you to swipe a month's worth of Item Shop cosmetics completely for free. It's a novel idea, but the community is already burning out, as dataminers have been unable to uncover the odds or how the system works, prompting speculation that Epic has been disabling tokens on the fly or that only a limited pool exists.

Finally, the official Fortnite Status account has disclosed the drop rates and put the speculation to bed: you have a 1 in 137,500 chance of finding a token.

"You asked for info on drop rates, so here's how it works. The new treasure this season is found in chests just like other items," Epic explained. "Treasure drop rates from chests are constant since season launch and don't vary throughout the day, except during Treasure Hours. Other than Gizmos, you can't get the same treasure twice."

Fortnite launched the first Treasure Hours event on November 7, but made no mention of Pirate Shop tokens. The assumption was that the drop rate would be unaffected, but that isn't the case.

Epic Games has confirmed that Pirate Shop Access drop rates are boosted 1.5x during Treasure Hours, equivalent to roughly 1 in 91,667. However, these odds "may be higher in future Treasure Hours."

Epic’s big Item Shop gamble seems to have already paid off, with players flocking to get into Fortnite's new mini-season.

Indeed, during the second Treasure Hours event on November 7, between 9-11pm ET (2-4am in the UK), the Pirate Shop Access drop rates were boosted by 2x—1 in 68,750.

Interestingly, Pirate Shop Access isn't the rarest reward in the game. That honor goes to the weekly gold outfit, which only has a drop rate of 1 in 1,562,500. Though Epic has been a bit more generous when boosting the odds during Treasure Hours, increasing your chances of finding it by 7.5-10x.

So, now we know the odds, but people are still getting their wires crossed with how RNG works. This doesn't mean opening 137,500 chests will guarantee you a Pirate Shop token.

Every single time you open a chest, it's like buying a lottery ticket. That first chest has just as much chance of landing you a token as the last chest you open, and while the odds are unlikely to land in your favor, that's again how RNG works. Epic wasn't exactly going to hand out thousands of dollars worth of cosmetics to millions of players—though it definitely could have handled the rollout a bit better, and most of this probably could've been avoided by disclosing the odds day one.

#4241. 10 Soulslikes That Are Unexpected Masterpieces

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

Creating a new genre is quite difficult, and while that's not exactly what FromSoftware did, it certainly gave rise to a new generation of titles aptly categorized under the Soulslike label.

The reasons why this phenomenon emerged organically and without premeditation are plentiful, as are the numerous gems that its rise to popularity among developers has gifted us.

Gradually, the niche became a popular segment among creators and players, but even so, its expansion has been such that many creations, despite their quality, have flown under the radar of most.

Therefore, in order to give due recognition to those works that oscillate between being unknown and not properly appreciated, I invite you to read this list of ten Soulslikes that are unexpected masterpieces.

As a self-proclaimed devotee of boss rushes, especially given that they're always the most interesting aspect of any Soulslike, no amount of praise is enough to highlight Rubinite's current popularity.

Despite its branching nature, it features an engaging story that perfectly complements the gameplay, which isn't the sole focus of the title; rather, both elements work together to create a truly well-rounded experience.

However, it's clear that anyone playing Rubinite will do so for the bosses (or for its gorgeous pixel art), and in this department, it performs sensationally, with varied adversaries in both aesthetics and gimmicks that truly maximize the game's satisfying mechanics.

As one of the year's best indie games, it inevitably makes the list of the most outstanding Soulslikes, especially since it pleasantly surprised me even though I'd been eagerly awaiting its release since the day it was announced.

The so-called flow state is a subtle key to the excellence of a Soulslike, as the magnificent AI LIMIT demonstrates through its simple yet direct combat that truly manages to captivate you from the first touch.

I admit I'm usually wary of titles that share its visual style due to past bad experiences, though this game reversed my expectations with its solid gameplay, both in its design and execution.

AI LIMIT's game feel is the experience's highlight, with mesmerizing encounters that, while not at the most challenging end, strike a perfect balance between being challenging and never frustrating.

If your mind, like mine, unconsciously compares it to similar products within and outside Soulslikes, I recommend you completely dispel any doubts, as few other examples of the genre can offer this level of reward.

If you remember the feeling you had the first time you played a Soulsborne game, that pleasant wonder of being captivated as you discovered an expansive world brimming with majesty, then encountering Mohrta is a gift from heaven.

Despite the obvious gameplay differences, since the game is both an FPS and an ARPG, the sense of discovery is practically the same, generating indescribable joy when you come across a new weapon, enemy, area, or NPC.

Everything in the game is so bizarre yet charming that it's difficult to play it in short bursts, because what it really makes you want to do is burn the midnight oil while enjoying its unparalleled inventiveness in terms of story, worldbuilding, and design.

If you've played any other title from its developer, Scumhead, you can more or less imagine what Mohrta has in store, though I can already tell you that it's the best video game this eccentric creator has ever produced.

There's nothing more fitting for this season than being destroyed by the same boss fifty-seven times in a row.

While I always found Mortal Shell a fascinating exercise in imagination within a dark and obtuse fantasy setting, I always considered it merely good, nothing more, but I can't say the same for Mortal Shell II.

Coming from a first title that was rough around the edges and failed to fully convince, Cold Symmetry surpassed even the most optimistic predictions with a sequel that addresses its predecessor's every single flaw.

The enemies' legibility, ease of spatial awareness, combat's feel, orientation within the main content, level design's firmness... It's comparatively much more robust, and I'd be lying if I said I expected such a significant leap in quality.

Therefore, Mortal Shell II proved me wrong, and nothing could make me happier. That it belongs in the discussion of the best Soulslikes of all time is undeniable at this point, yet it doesn't rank higher on the list because I'm sure there were devotees who knew this would be the outcome.

Bloodborne is the kind of video game that, once you finish it, leaves you with the bittersweet feeling that you'll never experience anything like it again, but Vigil: The Longest Night comes pretty close.

Although its gameplay is much more tactical and careful than its 3D counterpart, its atmosphere is undeniably analogous, especially due to the artistic and narrative similarities that place both within the realm of cosmic and body horror.

From there on, the comparisons begin to diminish, as it's more reminiscent of Salt and Sanctuary in its combat and progression systems, though its founding elements are masterfully aligned with FromSoftware's prodigious child.

Therefore, Vigil: The Longest Night achieves a feat that very few others can: making you feel like you're playing Bloodborne. This might seem like a weak argument for calling it a masterpiece, but when you truly grasp the difficulty of such an undertaking, it's not so far-fetched after all.

If you haven't played Queen's Domain yet, be sure to leave this article open in another tab while you download it, because one of the most immersive games of 2026 awaits you.

If King's Field were released today, I'm sure it would strive to resemble the work of Freshly Baked Games LLC, whom I was honored to discover through their debut title, The New Flesh, and with whom I've been inseparable ever since.

The decision to follow their lead was the right one, as keeping an eye out for the release of their retro-fantasy action RPG has given me one of the year's finest experiences, especially since I love titles inspired by Dark Souls more for their level design, interconnectivity, and progression than for their combat systems.

Some might say that Queen's Domain isn't Soulslike enough because it aligns more with the philosophy than the practicalities, but for me, that's enough, as it's one of the most highly recommended and captivating games released in the last couple of months.

In these Soulslikes, studying your enemy and playing carefully is vital.

Soulslikes tend to be very traditional in terms of what they do and how they do it, but the arrival of an outsider to the genre like One More Level brought a breath of fresh air in the form of Valor Mortis.

As the creators of Ghostrunner, a first-person platformer that excels in its spectacular movement sequences, their ARPG inherited that skill to create the most enjoyable experience in the genre in terms of movement.

The levels are gigantic in scale and verticality, allowing you to fly through the air using a grappling hook, run along walls, and swing to ledges, giving it a completely unique feel that no other Soulslike has ever achieved.

Add to that combat that balances parries and dodges like Lies of P, spectacular and grotesque (though easy) bosses, and customization options that are limited but refined, and you realize that Valor Mortis is much more than what people say about it.

Considering they had just released the least-reviewed Darksiders game to date, nobody bet a penny on Gunfire Games' success with Remnant: From the Ashes, and yet nobody remained silent when it came to praising its remarkable quality.

Making a permanently cooperative title with third-person shooter mechanics in a sporadically online and predominantly melee branch is among the boldest moves the genre has ever seen, which is already quite an achievement.

Regardless, Remnant: From the Ashes doesn't stand out simply for its innovation; it's a robust and extremely fun game whose variety of weapons, bosses, and environments allows for a deep adventure, brimming with content that's worth experiencing in its entirety.

Its breakout performance is a bit of a blow to me, as I suspect that, over the years, they'll prioritize this IP over Darksiders, but if that's the sacrifice to keep getting the best co-op games in the genre... so be it.

The First Berserker: Khazan's announcement certainly didn't leave any avid fan indifferent, as it gave the impression of being a major beast within the genre, but I don't think anyone could have anticipated its true severity.

Although its average critical reception is more mixed, I'm more inclined to agree with the unanimous opinion of the gaming community that it's a serious contender to be FromSoftware's ultimate heir.

It's difficult to describe what you have to feel to comprehend it truly, but holding the controls while fighting The First Berserker: Khazan's bosses is an untamed magic that courses through your entire body, filling you with adrenaline and excitement that are tough to match.

Were it not for the somewhat simplistic nature of its basic enemies and environments, the discussion about the title would be very different, yet you forget all of that when you enter the zone of maximum concentration thanks to its diverse, refined, and satisfying gameplay.

Every genre has its defining features, and the Soulslike is one that gets misunderstood fairly often with games like these blurring the line.

The only reason I disagree with those who believe the previous Soulslike is the best of them all is due to Lies of P's existence, a title that no one even came close to predicting, even if today it is commonly recognized under said distinction.

When we talk about unexpected masterpieces, the fact that NEOWIZ, a company originally conceived to distribute music games for the PlayStation Portable, developed the only Soulslike capable of rivaling the originals is among the entire century's most unpredictable events.

No matter how much faith you had in its release, there was no way to imagine that Lies of P would have such a vast arsenal, iconic and demandingly engaging bosses, levels crafted to perfection, a spectacular soundtrack, and even a story that keeps you engaged until the very last second.

Add to that its worldbuilding, side quests, flawless combination of parries and dodges, level of customization through the weapon assembly system, masterful enemy positioning and shortcuts... and you're left with a title that can only be described as majestic.

Lies of P raised the bar for the genre to a new level, and since 2024, it has become the ultimate benchmark despite coming from such a modest and distant background as that of its creators.

From the indie ecosystem to productions approaching AAA measures, these are ten Soulslike franchises that should come back by 2027.

#4238. EA Reportedly Closed BioWare To Invest In Developing Star Wars Battlefront III Instead Of The Next Mass Effect

Electronic Arts shut down the legendary RPG studio BioWare last week, ending development on an untitled fifth Mass Effect game. Since then, we've seen what appears to be a leaked trailer for the game, which suggests it might have been called Mass Effect Universe, and heard a sneak peek at what Grammy-winning composer Austin Wintory was cooking up for the beloved sci-fi RPG series. Over the past week, fans across the internet have tried to piece together how a publisher could decide to shut down a studio as prolific as BioWare, but according to a new Bloomberg report, the answer is Star Wars.

More specifically, Bloomberg writes that, presented with the opportunity to develop Star Wars Battlefront III with Disney, the publisher, which went private last year after a $55 billion acquisition,  chose to invest its money into that instead of BioWare's in-development Mass Effect sequel. The publication writes that EA looked at its portfolio for the coming years and had two massive sci-fi investments it could continue: Star Wars Battlefront III or BioWare's next Mass Effect. Even though Mass Effect was well into development, and even though the Battlefront threequel hasn't even entered development, EA chose to continue with the latter. And so BioWare was shut down, and Mass Effect development ended, though Bloomberg's sources say there are other, less significant reasons the studio was shuttered, too.

Those other factors include the poor reception to 2017's Mass Effect: Andromeda, the failure of Anthem in 2019, and 2024's Dragon Age: The Veilguard, which, despite garnering positive critical reception, apparently missed EA's sales expectations by 50%.

There's also the uncomfortable reality that BioWare made progressive LGBTQIA+ positive games but was a studio within a publisher house now partially owned by the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia, a government fund from a country where same-sex activity, including marriage, is criminalized, sometimes punishable by death; these harsh laws extend to other facets of the LGBTQIA+ community. Another investment partner in this acquisition of EA is Affinity Partners, a Miami-based investment firm founded and run by former White House senior advisor Jared Kushner, who is the son-in-law of President Donald Trump, a political figure who imposes laws that discriminate against the LGBTQIA+ community, especially the 1% of Americans who are transgender; Trump has also been known to mock this community in various ways. No official statements say BioWare shut down because of its progressive leanings, but one has to wonder if that was a factor, especially after reports that BioWare scrubbed diversity from demos to avoid negative feedback from EA (thanks, Kotaku).

When BioWare closed last week, only 50 employees remained, all working on the next Mass Effect, after years of layoffs at the studio.

A Mass Effect TV series is still in the works at Amazon, even though EA seems to have hung up Commander Shepard's video game suit for good.

#4237. Tomorrow's Battlefield 6 patch somehow makes jets more useless, improves armor bar visibility in Redsec

The first Battlefield 6 patch of the year is almost here, bringing a smattering of changes, including one that doesn't quite make sense.

Battlefield 6’s promised, season-extending update has been officially detailed. The patch, version 1.1.3.5, arrives tomorrow, January 20 right when Season 1 was supposed to end. Part of the update’s goal is to extend the current season, until Season 2 kicks off in the middle of February.

Update 1.1.3.5 does, of course, have a change log of its own that goes beyond just the season’s extension, but the changes fall somewhere between not very exciting, and a bit puzzling.

Patch 1.1.3.5 is, for all intents and purposes, a smaller update. When Battlefield Studios announced it earlier last week, the developer didn’t promise any major changes or fixes, so expectations never got out of hand.

The patch is mainly made up of bug fixes, but it does have three key areas of improvements to gameplay. There’s a big focus on melee combat, how responsive/unresponsive it is with the various melee tools, and how melee behaviour interacts with sprinting and other animations.

The end result should be faster attack speeds for the knife, and clearer wind-up animations for both the knife and the sledgehammer. The timing dictating when melee damage gets credited has also been made more consistent in different environments.

Interestingly, sprint is now only interrupted when the melee attack reaches its target. As it stands, sprinting is only interrupted after the full duration of the animation has been completed, which adds to the that perceived feeling of sluggishness.

The other major, and arguably most confusing is the nerf to jet cannons. The patch is going to make jets far less stronger against other air vehicles, requiring 40% more hits to destroy a target. This is puzzling because jets - and air vehicles in general - are already the least survivable in Battlefield 6.

And, considering how the rest of a jet's arsenal is either situational or nearly ineffective, the cannons were really the one guaranteed way of downing other air vehicles, so long as you manage to land your shots consistently. While the change is wellmeaning, the percentage will likely be reduced in future patches.

Finally, the update makes a few refinements to UI across the game, though mainly aimed at Redsec and modes where players wear armor. Armor bar visibility has been improved, and there’s a fix for the annoying bug that sometimes caused the armor bar to disappear every few seconds.

#4233. Battlefield 6’s first big map in months is coming to Labs soon, but I'm more excited about BF4's Golmud Railway making its way to BF6

As promised, Battlefield Labs is coming back to bring us a preview of some of Battlefield 6’s upcoming Season 2 content.

Battlefield 6’s Season 2 was recently pushed back by a month to give Battlefield Studios time to polish up its content. Now, the developer has revealed how it plans to use some of that time, and the first port of call is Battlefield Labs.

As discussed in the initial delay message, BF Studios wants the community’s involvement earlier and more consistently in the development of future content. This includes Season 2, of course, and a big component of what it’s bringing to the game is headed to Labs.

The first Battlefield Labs session kicking off soon will focus on Contaminated, one of the new maps coming to Battlefield 6 with Season 2. BF Studios says the map falls between Eastwood and Mirak Valley, in terms of size.

The blog post even likened it to Battlefield 1’s St. Quentin Scar, and Battlefield 5’s Arras. Although we’ve yet to actually play it, the size and description do sound really well, especially in a game as starved of big maps as Battlefield 6 currently is.

Another thing BF Studios wants to test is the way ground vehicle gameplay and aerial presence interact with infantry combat, which is pretty standard for most Battlefield maps. Interestingly, there appears to be some sort of mechanic unique to Contaminated that the developer also wants to evaluate.

More Labs sessions are planned, including one that will show off new gameplay tools and vehicles. The AH-6 Little Bird helicopter was specifically namedropped, which makes sense given that it’s going to be part of Season 2’s content.

Battlefield Labs sessions will also extend beyond the biggest-ticket items of maps and vehicles. BF Studios said we should expect tests of upcoming features, like the Aircraft Radar, as part of a list of other air combat updates.

Ground vehicles, and they way the various rockets interact with them, will also be evaluated in a different session, with specific adjustments planned for RPGs and TOWs. And, of course, the work to improve and perfect hit reg remains ongoing, and future tweaks will go through Labs first.

There’s even more exciting news for fans of big maps, as the blog post also confirmed that Battlefield 4’s Golmud Railway is currently in the works, planned to go live in a future season. Golmud Railway will show up early in Labs, and you can expect it to evolve over multiple sessions.

For context, when it does arrive in Battlefield 6, Golmud Railway will be the largest map in the game, which is saying something. Though the map is beloved by vehicle players, it has its issues elsewhere, and BF Studios says it will be looking at all that when it creates the BF6, emphasising that it won’t be a simple port of the BF4 original.

Finally, the post throws a bone to Redsec battle royale players still waiting for a Solo mode. BF Studios continues to test the idea internally, but it’s taking a while. Needless to say, there are so many aspects that need to be considered. Game pace, balance, player survivability, match flow just to name a few.

Redsec BR was built with squads in mind, so that task is extra challenging. Though the developer didn’t say when we can expect Solos to arrive in Labs, players will get a chance to experience it before it enters the live game.

#4232. Arc Raiders finally reveals early 2026 roadmap, but we’re not getting a new map for a while

The first couple of months of 2026 in the world of Arc Raiders look pretty promising, but the big guns are being held back for now.

After weeks of waiting, Arc Raiders developer Embark has officially unveiled the first few months of the game’s 2026 roadmap. The plan is split into four months, covering January to April, collectively dubbed Escalation.

We’re expecting a content update each month, with the majority of the biggest additions happening on the game’s existing maps. There is, however, at least one new map in the works, but it won’t be here until sometime in April.

While we wait for that, Arc Raiders is going to go through several events and other in-game changes, some more meaningful (and exciting) than others. January looks to be the lightest so far, which makes sense given that it’s just a week or so from ending.

January’s chapter is titled Headwinds, kicking off on January 27. This segment will see the addition of a new matchmaking option for players above level 40 - at or near the game’s endgame. We’re also expecting a new Map Condition, and a new Player Project for everyone to contribute to.

Things start getting interesting in February, when Shrouded Sky will begin. This chapter brings three exciting additions to Arc Raiders. There will be a new Map Condition, new Arc Threat, and the start of another Player Project.

Interestingly, we’re going to see some sort of map update during the month, but Embark didn’t share anymore details. The next Raider Deck will also deploy in February, alongside a new Expedition Window.

The Flashpoint chapter begins in March, when we’re expecting another new Map Condition, one more new Arc Threat, as well as another Player Project. March’s most interesting addition is an update to everyone’s trusty rooster friend, Scrappy.

Finally, April is when the big guns come out, because that’s when the first new map of 2026 will arrive in Arc Raiders. With it, comes a new large Arc, which is to be expected. A new Map Condition will debut then, too, likely starting off on the new map.

That’s pretty much it, but seeing as we’re just one day away from the start of the January stage, things are about to get exciting again in Arc Raiders.

You’ll explore a vast world full of terrifying mechanised creatures and meet survivors who need your help. Build a shelter to protect your people and modify it to your heart's content using the remains of your colossal fallen foes. Train troops, capture and modify beasts, and form alliances as you journey across the wastes. As you progress, you'll build an army of beasts, including Scorchers, Spikerollers, and Sickleclaws.

#4229. Nioh 3’s generous demo is out now, and your progress carries over to the full game

If you’re looking for a way to check out one of the biggest releases of early 2026, Team Ninja has made it easy for you.

Nioh 3 is one of the most anticipated games of 2026, and it’s easily among the biggest releases of February. We’re a few days away from the start of that month, however, but we don’t have to wait until then to actually play Team Ninja’s next major release.

The previously announced demo has arrived, and it’s one any fan of action games should check out, especially if you missed the PlayStation-exclusive beta held last year.

Unlike previous tests, the Nioh 3 demo is available on PC and PS5, just like the main game. This is pretty new for the series, which has typically launched first on PlayStation before coming to PC months later.

The Nioh 3 demo includes a decent portion of content from the beginning of the game. It’s enough to show off the core duality mechanic, letting you switch between the Samurai and Ninja styles at will. It also includes a preview of the game’s open field level design, which makes it sit somewhere between full open world and the more linear level design of past Nioh games.

Feedback from the previous beta has been implemented into the demo (and full release), so you may see some familiar faces, as well as areas you visited before - assuming you played that one.

Another big reason why you might want to grab the Nioh 3 demo is that your progress in it will carry over to the full version. This includes the character creator, too, meaning you can spend all day perfecting your character without having to worry about missing out on playing the actual game.

The demo even supports online multiplayer for up to three players, in case you come to Nioh for co-op. If you complete the available content, you’ll earn an in-game bonus in the full version. This is something Team Ninja has done with past Nioh titles, of course.

This time, your reward is the Twin-Snake Helmet. Just make sure you complete the demo before February 15.

Nioh 3 is out February 6 on PC, and PlayStation 5.

#4227. The Top 10 Best Horror Games To Play This Halloween

Humans are drawn to horror in all forms, real life and fiction. Perhaps it’s the desire to get as close to death as possible without actually dying; perhaps it’s the morality of life and knowing death comes for all of us; perhaps all our heads are just a little miswired. Whatever the reason, we flock to movies where supernatural entities and puppets on tricycles upend otherwise lovely lives, TV shows where murderous cults kill and stump local detectives, and books where the words on the page seem to follow you to bed. Games, however, go a step further, letting you enter the horror and control it (or become its victim), and you could argue that, as a result, they’re the most immersive form of fiction.

We at Game Informer love a healthy dose of horror from time to time, and we often review games like this. Some terrify us. Others… don’t. And the best ones stick with us for years and years after the credits. Below is a list of 10 of the best horror games we’ve played recently. This isn’t an all-time list, so don’t fret if your personal favorite isn’t here. Instead, this is a collection of 10 horror games ordered by release date that we think are great for spooky season and beyond. Let us know in the comments what you would add to the list!

The cozy corner of the horror genre seems to have exploded overnight, and now tons of new slice-of-life horror games are in various stages of development. That said, the team behind newcomer The Village in the Shade is no stranger to the form; they made the Yomawari series, a cute-and-terrifying collection of creepy virtual tales. The Village in the Shade takes things back to the homestead, giving you (a child who emerged from a hole in the ground and was immediately given the responsibility of running an entire farm by yourself) the freedom to plant, sow, reap, ranch, and more. Just follow the important rules: don't go out at night, don't share secrets, and don't leave the village among others. You wouldn't want to break the rules, right? You could, theoretically, go about your idyllic rural living. But as you unravel the threads of what this village is, who you are, and why you're here, it's hard not to get drawn into the strange, mysterious, delightfully disturbing truths hiding in its shadows. Just don't forget to water your turnips before you go sneaking out again.

Fans of survival horror and old-school FMV adventure games will find plenty to love (and fear) in Tenebris Somnia. When a young woman visits her ex-boyfriend’s apartment and discovers he's trapped in a hellish dream world, it kicks off a well-executed survival-horror trek of inventive puzzles and resource management to overcome dangerous monsters. High-production, live-action cutscenes help tell the story of a deteriorating relationship and the toll an indie horror film took on its creators, and they play an important role in gameplay. Tenebris Somnia may not look like much due to its classic pixelated presentation, but its scares and story captivate. – Our Review

Resident Evil Requiem is not just one of the best Resident Evil games, but it’s also one of the best horror games ever made. It features a unique dual-protagonist structure. Grace Ashcroft is timid, new to the whole “shooting zombies in the head while dealing with Umbrella viruses” thing, and is generally just trying to do her job. Leon S. Kennedy, however, is a veteran of all that and more. Requiem splits its runtime between the two characters, letting you experience both sides of Capcom’s marquee survival-horror style. Grace’s sections leave your hands clammy and your blood pressure high as you desperately try to survive. Leon’s sections leave your hands shaking with adrenaline and your blood pumping with excitement as he mows down zombies (sometimes literally, courtesy of those pesky chainsaws). The result is a Resident Evil game that blends two typical RE experiences – terrifying and tough or exhilarating over-the-top action – into one cohesive package. It’s perfect for someone who wants to feel scared and then soon after receive the catharsis of being the one in control, like being the tragic victim who dies in Act One of the horror movie and the last one standing who lives to tell the tale. – Our Review

Little Nightmares developer Tarsier Studios has a knack for delivering creepy side-scrolling adventures, but Reanimal eschews any whimsy to become its scariest game yet. While mechanically it is similar to Little Nightmares and still puts small children in unimaginable peril, Reanimal is capital-H horror thanks largely to its terrifying threats and disturbing animal-themed imagery (this probably isn’t the game for animal lovers; some messed-up stuff happens to these critters). Escaping the game’s island setting is thrilling and chilling whether you’re playing alone or with a friend in co-op. Months after release, we’re still thinking about Reanimal’s memorable final sequence, which is worth the price of admission on its own. – Our Review

2001’s Silent Hill 2 is considered one of the best horror video games of all time for good reason. At release, it was a graphical powerhouse, using the PlayStation 2's horsepower to create a setting that begged to be explored, even though every bone in your body said you shouldn’t. The remake from developer Bloober Team took on a big task in modernizing the game without losing the original’s soul, and it did a great job. Among all the recent Silent Hill releases (Silent Hill f, Silent Hill: Townfall), the remake is our favorite. The story of James Sunderland and his troubling relationship with his departed wife is complex, emotional, and – important for the purposes of this list – unsettling and scary. – Our Review

Alan Wake 2 is an excellent pick for some spooky madness, in the vein of David Lynch’s seminal Twin Peaks mystery-surrealist series. Don’t worry too much about the “2” part of the game’s title. You just need to know that the titular Alan Wake character is a not-great writer who acts like he’s really great, his wife is missing, and he got trapped in the ambiguous Dark Place. He’s only one half of the Alan Wake 2 equation, with his segments set in a dream-like version of New York City. Playing as him feels the most Twin Peaks-y. The other half is Saga, a police officer who arrives in the Pacific Northwest town of Bright Falls to investigate a murder that might be linked to a cult. You can expect more traditional survival-horror gameplay from her. But this is still a Remedy Entertainment game, and without spoiling anything, it goes places. And along the way, you can expect plenty of scares. Turn the lights down low (or off), light a candle, and sit back and enjoy one of Remedy’s best games. – Our Review

Square Enix has gone two-for-two with its Paranormasight series, an anthology of stories about the strange and occult. And while the more recent Mermaid's Curse is a brilliant tale all its own, the first entry – The Seven Mysteries of Honjo – brings significantly more scares. A group of people in the city of Honjo find themselves caught in a spectral battle royale, using powerful objects and conditions to curse one another, with the allure of a prize at the end. Its magic isn't just in the flowchart timeline, where you can hop between different perspectives and protagonists to see how events play out from every angle, but also in the gorgeous stereoscopic environments and narrative puzzles. Adventure games are a classic genre, and Paranormasight will remind you of what the genre is capable of the moment you slowly spin your camera around, your eyes peeking out from behind your fingers.

Survival horror can contain multitudes, and as the years have worn on, the genre has grown to encompass a wide range of action-combat mechanics. Signalis feels like a re-centering in that respect. It's an isometric survival-horror indie project from developer rose-engine, filled with clever puzzles, scarce resources, limited inventory slots, and looming, oppressive dread. As the Replika unit Elster, you delve deep into a remote complex filled with horrors and monsters, searching for something, or someone, waiting down below. While love for classic horror games and other hallmarks of genre fiction will certainly draw you in, the stylish presentation and devastatingly human core will keep you forging ahead to the finale. Once you've breached the surface of Signalis' retro-future super-structures, you won't be able to turn back.

In horror movies, audiences often groan at a protagonist for putting themselves in seemingly grave danger just to learn more about a cursed amulet or bloodthirsty killer. But in Immortality, you are the protagonist, and despite a lingering sense that you shouldn't be digging into the archives of these abandoned films, each eerie new scene makes you want to dive deeper. It's a game about Marisa Marcel, an actress who almost starred in three movies in the late 20th century, but has since disappeared. None of the movies were ever released due to mysterious circumstances, but you have access to the archived, unedited live-action footage, including behind-the-scenes conversations. By scrubbing through footage, you can select people or items in each scene and jump to random footage from any other movie that includes the same person or item. The approach to puzzle-solving is unique and keeps you appropriately disoriented. The mystery at the center is an unsettling treat to unravel, and scary in new and unexpected ways. Immortality is one of a kind and an easy recommendation for horror fans who want to try something a little different.

In the decade since launch, Dead by Daylight has continued to succeed, thanks to a dedicated (and newcomer-friendly) fanbase and its towering roster of original and licensed personas from across pop culture horror. The asymmetrical multiplayer title has become an anthology of horror’s biggest faces, including Freddy Krueger, Ghostface, Pyramid Head, and even the Xenomorph. Whether you play as a Survivor, trying to escape all manner of nightmare locations through stealth and cunning, or as a Killer, whose experience feels more like a hunting club, you’ll understand why Dead by Daylight has become a recurring destination for fans of the gruesome and bizarre.

Read about the making of Dead by Daylight and how it sunk its teeth into millions of players in our six-page exclusive feature in Issue 368 (p. 42), available in our magazine archive to anyone with a free Game Informer account.

#4226. 10 Best GameCube JRPGs That You Need to Play in Fall 2026

Contributor at DualShockers, former Esports Insider DACH content lead, former Escapist Magazine Germany content lead, software engineering background.

There’s always a specific moment every year where I realise that autumn has properly arrived. The evenings start drawing in before I’ve even had the chance to notice, the air gets crisper, and my coffee suddenly needs to be hot enough to warm both hands around the mug. I don’t think of myself as someone who hibernates, but I’d be lying if I said I didn’t naturally start staying in a little more this time of year.

And honestly? I love it. Being cozied up on my sofa with a blanket, a hot drink and the rain doing its thing outside is one of my favourite feelings, and it always seems to pull me towards games that tug on my nostalgia heartstrings. More often than not, that means the GameCube. Its JRPG library was smaller than what you’d find on its competitors, but it was stranger, braver and far more charming than it ever got credit for.

So many GameCube games have managed to escape the console in some way, but there are some JRPGs still waiting to abandon ship.

Some of these games have since found their way onto modern hardware, whilst others are still very much living in 2004, waiting for you to dig out an old memory card. A couple of them are certified classics, a few are delightfully weird, and at least one asks you to keep a close eye on the expiry date of your bananas. So grab a blanket, put the kettle on, and let’s take a look at the ten GameCube JRPGs that deserve a spot in your autumn rotation.

Tales of Symphonia was a big deal for GameCube owners. Released in Japan in August 2003, before reaching North America in July 2004 and Europe that November, it was the first Tales game to make the jump into 3D, complete with gorgeous cel-shaded visuals and character designs by Kosuke Fujishima. You follow Lloyd Irving and his childhood friend Colette, the Chosen One, on a journey to regenerate the dying world of Sylvarant. Naturally, things turn out to be a lot more complicated than that.

What made it really special, though, was the multiplayer. Up to four people could plug in a controller and take over a party member in the real-time battles, even if the camera stubbornly stuck to player one, leaving everyone else to fend for themselves off-screen. Add in the optional skits you could trigger with the Z button and a soundtrack by Motoi Sakuraba, and you have a game that will happily eat 80 hours of your autumn. If digging out the original hardware isn’t for you, the 2023 remaster on Switch, PS4 and Xbox One is the easier way in.

Taking a franchise famous for its tight, side-scrolling action and turning it into a turn-based RPG sounds like a recipe for disaster. Capcom did it anyway in 2004, and the result is a wonderfully fun little oddity that also found its way onto the PlayStation 2. Set in the 23rd century, X, Zero and newcomer Shadow are sent to Giga City to put an end to a Reploid rebellion led by Epsilon, with everything revolving around a powerful new substance called Force Metal.

Battles are snappy, and Hyper Modes, which let your characters transform mid-fight for a temporary power boost, keep things from ever getting stale. Axl joins the fold along the way, as does a slick bounty hunter called Spider, and the cast as a whole has a lot more personality than I expected going in. It received a fairly average critical response at the time, but it sold well, and I think it has aged far better than its reputation suggests.

Baten Kaitos was developed by Monolith Soft and tri-Crescendo, published by Namco, and released in Japan in December 2003, before making its way west across 2004 and 2005. Its world is made up of islands floating high in the sky, with the oceans below reduced to nothing more than legend. Fittingly, the name comes from the Arabic for “belly of the whale”, and it’s also the name of a star in the constellation Cetus. You don’t play as the protagonist, Kalas, but as a Guardian Spirit bonded to him, and he will very happily talk to you directly.

Everything revolves around Magnus, cards that capture the essence of objects, and with over 1,000 of them, deck building gets intricate fast. The fun part? Many Magnus change in real time. Grapes go rotten, then turn into wine, then vinegar, and a perfectly good banana will eventually turn on you if you leave it sitting in your deck. The 2023 HD Remaster on Switch bundles it with its prequel, Baten Kaitos Origins, which is a lovely excuse to finally experience both.

Path of Radiance launched in 2005 as the ninth main entry in the series, but only the third to make it to the West. It was the first Fire Emblem on a home console since Thracia 776, and it brought a few firsts along with it: 3D maps, voice acting and full motion cutscenes. You take control of Ike, a young mercenary who ends up at the centre of a war on the continent of Tellius, where the human beorc and the half-human laguz share a long, complicated history of mistrust.

Ike went on to become one of the series’ most beloved characters, joining the roster of Super Smash Bros. Brawl and later topping the men’s side of the very first Choose Your Legends poll in Fire Emblem Heroes. Permadeath is, of course, still very much a thing, so be prepared for heartbreak if you get careless. Players with save data from the Game Boy Advance Fire Emblem games could even link up to unlock concept art and special maps, which is the kind of connectivity I often find myself missing nowadays.

For years, a physical copy cost an arm and a leg. Thankfully, it joined the GameCube library on Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack in January 2026, so if you own a Switch 2, there has never been an easier time to sign up with the Greil Mercenaries. And should you get hooked, Radiant Dawn on the Wii picks up the story afterwards.

Skies of Arcadia first set sail on the Dreamcast in 2000, but for many of us, Legends on the GameCube was where we first met Vyse, Aika and Fina. You play as a Blue Rogue, essentially a sky pirate with a moral compass, in a world of floating continents orbited by six moons. The Valuan Empire is hunting down the Moon Crystals, and it falls to you and your crew to stop them, mostly by being extremely charming about it.

Exploration is at the heart of everything. Sailing into the unknown, stumbling across Discoveries and selling the information for a reward is ridiculously satisfying, and Legends bumped the total up to 89. The port also added Moonfish to hunt down and a bounty hunter named Piastol, whose side story finally explains how Vyse got that scar on his face. Crucially, it also toned down the random encounter rate, which anyone who survived the Dreamcast version will deeply appreciate.

If you're looking for some rough times on the Gamecube, here are 8 hard to beat Gamecube JRPGs.

Long before Demon’s Souls, FromSoftware made a card-based action RPG for the GameCube. Known as Rune in Japan, Lost Kingdoms released there in April 2002, with Activision publishing it in North America and Europe later that year. It was one of the very first JRPGs on the GameCube, and it shows in the best possible way: it’s a little rough, a little ambitious, and absolutely its own thing.

You play as Princess Katia, tasked with saving the five kingdoms of Argwyll from a mysterious fog that is swallowing the land. Instead of swinging a sword, you build a deck of cards, each one summoning a creature or weapon in real time, which makes every encounter feel like a frantic little puzzle. There’s even a two-player mode where you can pit your deck against a friend’s.

Reviews were average at the time, but it did well enough to get a sequel, Lost Kingdoms II, set 200 years later. Looking back now, it’s fascinating to see the studio already leaning into melancholy, fog-drenched fantasy a whole seven years before it would change everything. It’s not the most polished game on this list, but it might just be the most interesting.

The Thousand-Year Door released in 2004 and is still, for many, the high point of the Paper Mario series. After Princess Peach sends Mario a treasure map and promptly goes missing, he ends up in Rogueport, a rather grimy town sitting on top of a legendary door, and sets out to find the seven Crystal Stars. Along the way, you’ll pick up a wonderful cast of partners, from know-it-all Goombella to Admiral Bobbery, a retired sailor who just so happens to be a Bob-omb.

Battles take place on a literal stage in front of an audience, who can cheer you on, throw items at you or bring the set crashing down. Every chapter feels like a different genre, whether that’s climbing the ranks in the Glitz Pit wrestling arena or solving a whodunnit aboard the Excess Express. Meanwhile, Peach is on her own little adventure with a computer called TEC-XX, and the interludes where you take control of Bowser are pure comedic gold. If you’d rather not hunt down a GameCube copy, the 2024 Switch remake is a gorgeous way to play.

Pokémon Colosseum turned the formula on its head. There are no wild Pokémon to catch, no gyms to conquer, and instead of a wide-eyed kid, you play as Wes, a former member of Team Snagem who kicks off the game by blowing up their hideout. Set in the desert region of Orre, you use a Snag Machine to steal Shadow Pokémon, whose hearts have been closed off by Team Cipher, straight from other trainers.

Every battle is a double battle, you start with Espeon and Umbreon, and slowly purifying your Shadow Pokémon by fighting alongside them is a surprisingly heartfelt gameplay loop. In North America, pre-ordering the game got you a bonus disc that let you send a Jirachi to your copy of Ruby or Sapphire, which also fixed the infamous berry glitch. Europe, sadly, didn’t get one.

It sold 2.41 million copies worldwide, and its sequel, Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness, joined the Switch 2’s GameCube library earlier this year. Colosseum was announced for the same service back in April 2025, and as of writing, we are still waiting for a release date. Patience is a virtue, or so they keep telling me.

Evolution Worlds is a curious one. Developed by Sting and published by Ubisoft outside of Japan, it arrived in 2002 as a compilation of two Dreamcast games, packing an abbreviated version of Evolution: The World of Sacred Device and the full Evolution 2: Far Off Promise onto one GameCube disc. Both games also received newly recorded English voice acting.

You play as Mag Launcher, a young adventurer exploring ancient ruins with a Cyframe, a powerful tool left behind by a long-lost civilisation. At its core, this is a turn-based dungeon crawler, and a genuinely charming one at that. It also has some of the most gloriously unhinged character names I’ve ever come across: Mag is joined by Linear Cannon, Chain Gun, Pepper Spray and his ever-loyal butler, Gre Nade.

I won’t pretend it’s the deepest game on this list. It really isn’t. But sometimes all you want on a rainy evening is a straightforward dungeon crawl with a lot of heart, and Evolution Worlds delivers exactly that. It’s comfort food in JRPG form, and there’s absolutely nothing wrong with that.

Final Fantasy Crystal Chronicles was a big moment, being the first Final Fantasy on a Nintendo home console since Final Fantasy VI back in 1994. Its world is covered in a poisonous miasma, and every village relies on a crystal to keep it at bay. Once a year, each village sends out a caravan to collect myrrh from distant trees, carrying a crystal chalice to protect them along the way, which many fans affectionately call the bucket.

The real hook was its multiplayer, and the price tag that came with it. Up to four players could join in, but every single one of them needed a Game Boy Advance and a link cable to act as their controller and personal screen. It was ambitious, a little bit impractical, and an absolute blast if you managed to pull it off. Playing solo, a Moogle carries the chalice for you instead.

You create your own caravanner from one of four tribes, the Clavat, Lilty, Yuke or Selkie, and set off into a world that rewards slow, patient journeys. If wrangling four GBAs sounds like a bit much, the 2020 Remastered Edition added online multiplayer, so your friends can join from the comfort of their own sofas. The myrrh only needs collecting once a year, after all.

Even though the GameCube didn't have a massive library, it did feature several fun and ambitious JRPG adventures.
